extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, applicants, patent office staff, and IP policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/practical standards for deciding when a claimed method (diagnostic/imaging/other) is excluded from patentability under the European Patent Convention as a 'method for treatment of the human or animal body by surgery'. Focuses on interpretation, scope, and claim-drafting consequences of Article 52(4)/53(c) EPC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of one surgical step excludes method from patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of one surgical step in a multi-step method is sufficient to exclude the method from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EBoA: A multi-step method that 'comprises or encompasses at least one feature defining a physical activity or action that constitutes a method step for treatment of a human or animal body by surgery or therapy' falls under the prohibition of Article 52(4)/53(c) EPC. Point of significance: the decision will exclude patenting of a multi-step method that comprises one step that is therapeutic, diagnostic or surgical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim falls under prohibition if it includes at least one physical intervention step
rubrics_metrics.description: A method claim falls under the prohibition of patenting methods for treatment by therapy or surgery if it comprises or encompasses at least one feature defining a physical activity or action that constitutes a method step for treatment of a human or animal body by surgery or therapy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims for any feature that is a physical intervention on the body. If such a feature is present, the claim is caught by the exclusion regardless of other non-surgical steps in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion not limited to therapeutic/curative surgery
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusion of treatments by surgery is not limited to surgery for a therapeutic purpose; 'treatment by surgery' is not confined to surgical methods pursuing a therapeutic purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EBoA rejected limiting 'surgery' to operations aimed at maintaining or restoring health. Legal history and the object/purpose of Article 53(c) EPC do not justify reading the term narrowly to therapeutic-only activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining scope of 'treatment by surgery' — professional skill and substantial health risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical interventions on the body that require professional medical skills and that entail a substantial health risk even when carried out with required professional care and expertise are covered by the exclusion of treatment by surgery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EBoA distinguished such interventions from 'safe routine techniques' or minor invasive interventions with no substantial health risks, which would go beyond the purpose of the exclusion. Example given: an injection into the heart (contrast agent) is an invasive step representing a substantial physical intervention requiring professional expertise and entailing health risk, and thus is excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine/minor invasive techniques may fall outside the exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluding from patentability safe routine techniques, even when of invasive nature, appears to go beyond the purpose of the exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an invasive step is minor, involves no substantial health risk and does not require significant professional medical skill, the ratio legis of Article 53(c) may not apply and the step may not render the claim unpatentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation principle for exclusion clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusion clauses should be interpreted using ordinary meaning and by reference to the object and purpose of the provision; the Vienna Convention does not mandate a blanket ‘narrower interpretation’ for exclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EBoA: Rules of interpretation require looking at ordinary meaning and object and purpose, and interpreting provisions so they take full effect. The fact that a provision is an exclusion is only one factor and does not by itself require a narrower interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction/amendment can avoid excluded subject-matter if essential features are specified
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim can be construed in a manner that avoids subject-matter excluded from patent protection provided the claims explicitly specify all of the essential features needed to define the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EBoA confirmed (relying on G‑1/04) that applicants may present/amend claims to avoid therapeutic/diagnostic/surgical steps, but must disclose all essential features. The EBoA anticipates that rules on disclosure of essential features will prevent undue attempts to claim what is otherwise excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods usable in surgical context are not per se surgical
rubrics_metrics.description: The possible use of a non-surgical method in a surgical method does not result in the non-surgical method being excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EBoA: A claimed imaging method is not to be considered a 'treatment of the human or animal body by surgery' merely because during a surgical intervention the data obtained by the method immediately allow a surgeon to decide on the course of action. Article 53(c) prohibits patenting surgical methods, not methods that can be used in the context of carrying out a surgical method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratio legis: socio-ethical objective behind the exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The object/purpose (ratio legis) of the exclusion is a socio-ethical consideration to free the medical profession from possible constraints imposed on them by patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy aim must be borne in mind when determining the scope of the exclusion and balancing who may be affected by allowing patents on medical/surgical procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical test for exclusion includes whether maintaining life/health is important and an invasive step is present
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed method in which, when carried out, maintaining the life and health of the subject is important and which comprises or encompasses an invasive step representing a substantial physical intervention on the body that requires professional medical expertise and entails a substantial health risk is excluded from patentability as a method for treatment by surgery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this conjunctive factual test (importance of maintaining life/health + invasive step requiring expertise + substantial health risk) when evaluating borderline diagnostic/imaging methods that may be integral to treatment decisions.
